claim: SCML2 is a mammalian homolog of Drosophila SCM, a Polycomb-group protein that associates with PRC1.
source: SCML2 is a mammalian homolog of Drosophila SCM, a Polycomb-group protein that associates with PRC1.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work on SCM and PRC1 interactions.

claim: SCML2A is an SCML2 isoform tightly associated to chromatin.
source: SCML2A, an SCML2 isoform tightly associated to chromatin, contributes to PRC1 localization and also directly enforces repression of certain Polycomb target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through biochemical fractionation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SCML2A contributes to PRC1 localization.
source: SCML2A, an SCML2 isoform tightly associated to chromatin, contributes to PRC1 localization and also directly enforces repression of certain Polycomb target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing decreased BMI1 occupancy upon SCML2AΔRBR overexpression (Figure 5).

claim: SCML2A directly enforces repression of certain Polycomb target genes.
source: SCML2A, an SCML2 isoform tightly associated to chromatin, contributes to PRC1 localization and also directly enforces repression of certain Polycomb target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by luciferase reporter assays (Figure 4C) and RNA-seq data showing gene derepression upon SCML2 knockdown without loss of BMI1 (Figure 7).

claim: SCML2A binds to PRC1 via its SPM domain.
source: SCML2A binds to PRC1 via its SPM domain and interacts with ncRNAs through a novel RNA-binding region (RBR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data showing that SCML2A but not SCML2B (which lacks the SPM domain) co-purifies with PRC1 components (Figure 4A).

claim: SCML2A interacts with ncRNAs through a novel RNA-binding region (RBR).
source: SCML2A binds to PRC1 via its SPM domain and interacts with ncRNAs through a novel RNA-binding region (RBR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RIP experiments (Figure 1A) and in vitro RNA binding assays (Figure 1C, Figure 2).

claim: Targeting of SCML2A to chromatin involves the coordinated action of the MBT domains, RNA binding, and interaction with PRC1 through the SPM domain.
source: Targeting of SCML2A to chromatin involves the coordinated action of the MBT domains, RNA binding, and interaction with PRC1 through the SPM domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by salt fractionation experiments showing that deletion of the RBR or mutation of the MBT domain reduces chromatin association (Figure 3).

claim: Deletion of the RBR reduces the occupancy of SCML2A at target genes.
source: Deletion of the RBR reduces the occupancy of SCML2A at target genes and overexpression of a mutant SCML2A lacking the RBR causes defects in PRC1 recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data comparing SCML2A WT and ΔRBR (Figure 5).

claim: Overexpression of a mutant SCML2A lacking the RBR causes defects in PRC1 recruitment.
source: Deletion of the RBR reduces the occupancy of SCML2A at target genes and overexpression of a mutant SCML2A lacking the RBR causes defects in PRC1 recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing decreased BMI1 occupancy in cells expressing SCML2AΔRBR (Figure 5).

claim: PcG mutants fail to maintain transcriptional repression of differentiation genes during development.
source: PcG mutants fail to maintain transcriptional repression of differentiation genes during development, which results in their ectopic expression, compromised patterning of the embryo, and homeotic transformations (Lewis, 1978; Struhl, 1981; Simon et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: SCM is required for appropriate body patterning during embryonic development in Drosophila.
source: One of these proteins is sex comb on midleg (SCM), which is required for appropriate body patterning during embryonic development in Drosophila (Simon et al., 1992; Bornemann et al., 1996, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: SCM and its human homologs were recovered in sub-stoichiometric amounts after biochemical purifications of the PRC1 complex.
source: SCM and its human homologs were recovered in sub-stoichiometric amounts after biochemical purifications of the PRC1 complex (Shao et al., 1999; Levine et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2012), suggesting a functional link between SCM and PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The MBT domain functions as a binding module for methylated lysines on histones.
source: SCM also belongs to a small family of proteins characterized by the presence of a conserved malignant brain tumor domain (MBT), which functions as a binding module for methylated lysines on histones (Bonasio et al., 2010a), further suggesting that SCM might function on chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior structural/biochemical work.

claim: SCM contains a C-terminal SPM domain through which it is thought to interact with PRC1.
source: In addition to the MBT domain, SCM contains a C-terminal SPM domain, through which it is thought to interact with PRC1 (Peterson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila, arrays of DNA motifs recognized by a variety of transcription factors function as recruitment 'hubs' for PRCs and are known as Polycomb responsive elements (PREs).
source: In Drosophila, arrays of DNA motifs recognized by a variety of transcription factors function as recruitment 'hubs' for PRCs and are known as Polycomb responsive elements (PREs) (Müller and Kassis, 2006); however, PREs alone are not sufficient to explain or predict the genome-wide occupancy patterns of PcG complexes (Simon and Kingston, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PREs alone are not sufficient to explain or predict the genome-wide occupancy patterns of PcG complexes.
source: In Drosophila, arrays of DNA motifs recognized by a variety of transcription factors function as recruitment 'hubs' for PRCs and are known as Polycomb responsive elements (PREs) (Müller and Kassis, 2006); however, PREs alone are not sufficient to explain or predict the genome-wide occupancy patterns of PcG complexes (Simon and Kingston, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Only a few examples of PRE-like DNA elements have been described in mammals to date.
source: In mammals, our understanding of PRC targeting is even more limited, given that only a few examples of PRE-like DNA elements have been described to date (Bengani et al., 2013; Cuddapah et al., 2012; Sing et al., 2009; Woo et al., 2010, 2013) and several of the transcription factors that bind and recruit Drosophila PRCs are absent or poorly conserved (Schuettengruber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several of the transcription factors that bind and recruit Drosophila PRCs are absent or poorly conserved in mammals.
source: In mammals, our understanding of PRC targeting is even more limited, given that only a few examples of PRE-like DNA elements have been described to date (Bengani et al., 2013; Cuddapah et al., 2012; Sing et al., 2009; Woo et al., 2010, 2013) and several of the transcription factors that bind and recruit Drosophila PRCs are absent or poorly conserved (Schuettengruber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: There are several mammalian versions of the two best characterized Drosophila PcG complexes, PRC1 and PRC2, which differ in subunit composition and chromatin localization.
source: Moreover, there are several mammalian versions of the two best characterized Drosophila PcG complexes, PRC1 and PRC2, which differ in subunit composition and chromatin localization (Kuzmichev et al., 2004; Margueron et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mammalian PRC1 closest in subunit composition to their Drosophila homolog are PRC1.2 and PRC1.4.
source: The mammalian PRC1 closest in subunit composition to their Drosophila homolog (PRC1.2 and PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]) have conserved functions in development and disease (Richly et al., 2011) and contain subunits that recognize trimethylated lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3), the catalytic product of PRC2 (Cao et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PRC1.2 and PRC1.4 have conserved functions in development and disease.
source: The mammalian PRC1 closest in subunit composition to their Drosophila homolog (PRC1.2 and PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]) have conserved functions in development and disease (Richly et al., 2011) and contain subunits that recognize trimethylated lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3), the catalytic product of PRC2 (Cao et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PRC1.2 and PRC1.4 contain subunits that recognize trimethylated lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3), the catalytic product of PRC2.
source: The mammalian PRC1 closest in subunit composition to their Drosophila homolog (PRC1.2 and PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]) have conserved functions in development and disease (Richly et al., 2011) and contain subunits that recognize trimethylated lysine 27 of histone H3 (H3K27me3), the catalytic product of PRC2 (Cao et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The genome-wide distribution of PRC1 is largely unchanged in embryonic stem cells that do not have H3K27me3.
source: Although H3K27me3 may contribute to stabilizing some forms of PRC1 on chromatin, the genome-wide distribution of PRC1 is largely unchanged in embryonic stem cells that do not have H3K27me3 (Tavares et al., 2012), and many PRC1 complexes do not contain the subunit that binds to H3K27me3 (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Many PRC1 complexes do not contain the subunit that binds to H3K27me3.
source: Although H3K27me3 may contribute to stabilizing some forms of PRC1 on chromatin, the genome-wide distribution of PRC1 is largely unchanged in embryonic stem cells that do not have H3K27me3 (Tavares et al., 2012), and many PRC1 complexes do not contain the subunit that binds to H3K27me3 (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RUNX1 has been proposed to guide PRC1 recruitment in specific contexts.
source: Various factors, including RUNX1 (Yu et al., 2012) and the RNA helicase MOV10 (El Messaoudi-Aubert et al., 2010), have also been proposed to guide PRC1 recruitment in specific contexts, but an overarching model remains lacking.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The RNA helicase MOV10 has been proposed to guide PRC1 recruitment in specific contexts.
source: Various factors, including RUNX1 (Yu et al., 2012) and the RNA helicase MOV10 (El Messaoudi-Aubert et al., 2010), have also been proposed to guide PRC1 recruitment in specific contexts, but an overarching model remains lacking.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: At least one ncRNA has been shown to make contact with PRC1.
source: Given that increasing evidence points to a role for noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) in mediating recruitment of chromatin complexes (Koziol and Rinn, 2010; Wang and Chang, 2011) and that at least one ncRNA has been shown to make contact with PRC1 (Yap et al., 2010), we hypothesized that an RNA-binding chromatin protein may be involved in PRC1 recruitment in mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila SCM is recruited to the PRE upstream of Ultrabithorax independent of PRC1 or PRC2.
source: A recent study showed that Drosophila SCM is recruited to the PRE upstream of Ultrabithorax independent of PRC1 or PRC2, whereas PRC1 and PRC2 binding requires the presence of SCM (Wang et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PRC1 and PRC2 binding to the PRE upstream of Ultrabithorax requires the presence of SCM.
source: A recent study showed that Drosophila SCM is recruited to the PRE upstream of Ultrabithorax independent of PRC1 or PRC2, whereas PRC1 and PRC2 binding requires the presence of SCM (Wang et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The human genome comprises four genes with homology to Scm.
source: The human genome comprises four genes with homology to Scm, but only two that contain conserved MBT, SPM, and DUF3588 domains, SCMH1 and SCML2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Only two human genes with homology to Scm contain conserved MBT, SPM, and DUF3588 domains: SCMH1 and SCML2.
source: The human genome comprises four genes with homology to Scm, but only two that contain conserved MBT, SPM, and DUF3588 domains, SCMH1 and SCML2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on genomic analysis.

claim: SCMH1 functions in spermatogenesis.
source: SCMH1 functions in spermatogenesis (Takada et al., 2007), whereas little is known about SCML2, except that it is ubiquitously expressed and that deletions of its coding sequence are found in a subset of medulloblastomas (Northcott et al., 2009), suggesting it may have tumor-suppressive activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SCML2 is ubiquitously expressed.
source: SCMH1 functions in spermatogenesis (Takada et al., 2007), whereas little is known about SCML2, except that it is ubiquitously expressed and that deletions of its coding sequence are found in a subset of medulloblastomas (Northcott et al., 2009), suggesting it may have tumor-suppressive activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Deletions of SCML2 coding sequence are found in a subset of medulloblastomas.
source: SCMH1 functions in spermatogenesis (Takada et al., 2007), whereas little is known about SCML2, except that it is ubiquitously expressed and that deletions of its coding sequence are found in a subset of medulloblastomas (Northcott et al., 2009), suggesting it may have tumor-suppressive activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SCML2 may have tumor-suppressive activity.
source: SCMH1 functions in spermatogenesis (Takada et al., 2007), whereas little is known about SCML2, except that it is ubiquitously expressed and that deletions of its coding sequence are found in a subset of medulloblastomas (Northcott et al., 2009), suggesting it may have tumor-suppressive activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a suggestion based on the observation of deletions in medulloblastomas.

claim: SCML2 co-purified with a relatively large amount of RNA compared to EZH2 and MLL.
source: We observed that the PcG protein SCML2, a homolog of Drosophila SCM, consistently co-purified with a relatively large amount of RNA, especially when compared to EZH2 and MLL, which are part of complexes known to interact with ncRNAs (Rinn et al., 2007; Kaneko et al., 2010, 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RIP experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SCML2 did not co-precipitate with either EZH2 or MLL or vice versa.
source: SCML2 did not co-precipitate with either EZH2 or MLL or vice versa (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on unpublished data.

claim: Amino acids 256–330 of SCML2 were necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro.
source: RNA binding assays with total HeLa S3 RNA and recombinant fragments of SCML2 (Figure 1B) revealed that amino acids 256–330 were necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the in vitro RNA binding assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SCML2 RBR exhibited little specificity for RNA sequence but discriminated between RNA and DNA in vitro.
source: Because the region spanning 256–330 bears no resemblance to other known RNA-binding domains, we tentatively refer to it as the RNA binding region (RBR) of SCML2. The SCML2 RBR exhibited little specificity for RNA sequence, but discriminated between RNA and DNA in vitro (Figure 1D), and strongly preferred single-stranded to double-stranded RNA (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The SCML2 RBR strongly preferred single-stranded to double-stranded RNA.
source: The SCML2 RBR exhibited little specificity for RNA sequence, but discriminated between RNA and DNA in vitro (Figure 1D), and strongly preferred single-stranded to double-stranded RNA (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SCML2 fragments lacking the RBR (ΔRBR) failed to bind any of the nucleic acids tested.
source: SCML2 fragments lacking the RBR (ΔRBR) failed to bind any of the nucleic acids tested (Figure 1D, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The RBR shifted both HOTAIR RNA and DNA in EMSA experiments.
source: The RBR shifted both HOTAIR RNA and DNA (Figure 2A), and so did the larger MBT-DUF fragment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but only HOTAIR RNA and not DNA competed efficiently for binding to the RBR (Figure 2B) or to the MBT-DUF fragments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only HOTAIR RNA and not DNA competed efficiently for binding to the RBR.
source: The RBR shifted both HOTAIR RNA and DNA (Figure 2A), and so did the larger MBT-DUF fragment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but only HOTAIR RNA and not DNA competed efficiently for binding to the RBR (Figure 2B) or to the MBT-DUF fragments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the competition EMSA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The RBR displayed an affinity for nucleosome particles, but much lower than for RNA.
source: The RBR displayed an affinity for nucleosome particles (Figure 2A), but much lower than for RNA as demonstrated by the fact that nucleosomes could not compete with HOTAIR RNA for binding to the RBR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Nucleosomes could not compete with HOTAIR RNA for binding to the RBR.
source: The RBR displayed an affinity for nucleosome particles (Figure 2A), but much lower than for RNA as demonstrated by the fact that nucleosomes could not compete with HOTAIR RNA for binding to the RBR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the competition EMSA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The RBR is capable of forming a ternary complex with nucleosomes and RNA simultaneously.
source: When both nucleosomes and RNA were present in limiting amounts, we noticed the appearance of a super-shifted band that was not observed when either species were added separately (Figure 2C, asterisk), suggesting that the RBR—and therefore SCML2—is capable of forming a ternary complex with nucleosomes and RNA simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 2C and pull-down data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The appearance of the super-shifted band was not due to GST-mediated dimerization.
source: The appearance of the super-shifted band was not due to GST-mediated dimerization, as it also occurred after the removal of the GST moiety from the RBR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Nucleosomes co-precipitated in vitro with both the SCML2 RBR and HOTAIR simultaneously.
source: The possibility of ternary complex formation is further supported by the observation that nucleosomes co-precipitated in vitro with both the SCML2 RBR and HOTAIR simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), whereas HOTAIR alone did not bind nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the pull-down data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: HOTAIR alone did not bind nucleosomes.
source: The possibility of ternary complex formation is further supported by the observation that nucleosomes co-precipitated in vitro with both the SCML2 RBR and HOTAIR simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), whereas HOTAIR alone did not bind nucleosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In vitro-transcribed RNA from the 601 nucleosome-positioning template competed less efficiently for binding to the RBR as compared to HOTAIR.
source: Not all RNA sequences were bound by the RBR to the same extent. In vitro-transcribed RNA from the 601 nucleosome-positioning template competed less efficiently for binding to the RBR as compared to HOTAIR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the competition EMSA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only the full 1–300 fragment of HOTAIR bound to the SCML2 RBR with sufficient affinity to co-precipitate, whereas none of the isolated stem-loops did.
source: We also tested the binding specificity of the SCML2 RBR for isolated stem-loops within the 5′ fragment of the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) HOTAIR that interacts with PRC2 (Tsai et al., 2010). Only the full 1–300 fragment bound to the SCML2 RBR with sufficient affinity to co-precipitate, whereas none of the isolated stem-loops did (data not shown), suggesting that the RBR is capable of recognizing complex structures and/or sequences and that it does not just form non-specific interactions with any type of RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on unpublished data.

claim: The human SCML2 locus gives rise to two alternative isoforms: SCML2A (full-length) and SCML2B (C-terminal truncation generated by alternative splicing).
source: As we reported previously, the human SCML2 locus gives rise to two alternative isoforms: one encodes the full-length version (SCML2A) and the other a C-terminal truncation, generated by alternative splicing (SCML2B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Lecona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to prior work and a schematic in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SCML2A is enriched in the chromatin fraction, whereas the bulk of SCML2B is found in the soluble nuclear fraction.
source: Although both SCML2 isoforms are predominantly nuclear, SCML2A is enriched in the chromatin fraction, whereas the bulk of SCML2B, which lacks the SPM domain is found in the soluble nuclear fraction, where it interacts with the cell cycle machinery and participates in the G1/S checkpoint (Lecona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SCML2B interacts with the cell cycle machinery and participates in the G1/S checkpoint.
source: Although both SCML2 isoforms are predominantly nuclear, SCML2A is enriched in the chromatin fraction, whereas the bulk of SCML2B, which lacks the SPM domain is found in the soluble nuclear fraction, where it interacts with the cell cycle machinery and participates in the G1/S checkpoint (Lecona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: An SCML2A mutant lacking the RBR (SCML2AΔRBR) was displaced from chromatin.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, an SCML2A mutant lacking the RBR (SCML2AΔRBR) was displaced from chromatin, as demonstrated by the fact that a larger fraction of this protein was released with low-salt extraction when compared to the wild-type (WT) form, regardless of the amount of transgenic protein being expressed (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Mutation of the acidic residue that coordinates the methylated lysine within the aromatic cage of the MBT domain resulted in loss of SCML2A from the chromatin fraction, but not to the extent observed with the RBR deletion.
source: We then assessed the potential role of the MBT domains in binding to chromatin. Mutation of the acidic residue that coordinates the methylated lysine within the aromatic cage impairs its binding (Sathyamurthy et al., 2003; Grimm et al., 2007; Santiveri et al., 2008) and also resulted in loss of SCML2A from the chromatin fraction, but not to the extent observed with the RBR deletion (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SCML2B displayed a predominantly diffuse distribution within the nucleus, which was not affected by the removal of the RBR.
source: The SCML2 isoform lacking the SPM domain, SCML2B, displayed a predominantly diffuse distribution within the nucleus, which was not affected by the removal of the RBR; however the residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation and microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-G.

claim: The residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR.
source: The SCML2 isoform lacking the SPM domain, SCML2B, displayed a predominantly diffuse distribution within the nucleus, which was not affected by the removal of the RBR; however the residual amount of SCML2B that could be recovered from the chromatin fraction was further decreased upon deletion of the RBR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-G.

claim: The affinity of SCML2 for chromatin is regulated by multiple molecular mechanisms, including binding to PRC1 via the SPM domain, histone marks via the MBT domains, and RNA via the RBR.
source: Together, these results show that the affinity of SCML2 for chromatin is regulated by multiple molecular mechanisms, including binding to PRC1 via the SPM domain, histone marks via the MBT domains, and RNA via the RBR.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the fractionation experiments.

claim: GFP–SCML2A accumulated in the nucleus and exhibited a punctate distribution.
source: Similar to the endogenous SCML2 protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), GFP–SCML2A accumulated in the nucleus and exhibited a punctate distribution, suggestive of recruitment to specific sub-nuclear compartments, presumably target sites on chromatin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GFP-SCML2AΔRBR exhibited a diffuse nuclear distribution.
source: In contrast, GFP-SCML2AΔRBR exhibited a diffuse nuclear distribution (Figure 3F) consistent with its looser association with chromatin revealed by biochemical fractionations (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The number of intense GFP spots decreased from a median value of 39 per cell for SCML2A to only 5 per cell for SCML2AΔRBR.
source: The number of intense GFP spots decreased from a median value of 39 per cell for SCML2A to only 5 per cell for SCML2AΔRBR (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Deletion of the RBR did not affect the ability of SCML2A to be imported into the nucleus.
source: Deletion of the RBR did not affect the ability of SCML2A to be imported into the nucleus, nor its ability to interact with other protein factors, including the core subunits of the PRC1 complex (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the microscopy data (Figure 3F) and mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4.
source: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4 (a subunit specific for PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]), suggesting that deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
source: Both SCML2AWT and SCML2AΔRBR co-purified with all the components of the canonical PRC1, including RING1A, RING1B, CBX2/8, PHC2/3, and BMI1/PCGF4 (a subunit specific for PRC1.4 [Gao et al., 2012]), suggesting that deletion of the RBR does not affect the ability of SCML2A to interact with PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only small traces of PRC1 components could be detected among the SCML2B-associated proteins.
source: Only small traces of PRC1 components could be detected among the SCML2B-associated proteins, despite the fact that a comparable number of SCML2 peptides were detected in the two purifications (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SCML2A co-purified with SCMH1 and L3MBTL3, both of which comprise C-terminal SPM domains.
source: SCML2A also co-purified with SCMH1 (the other SCM homolog in humans) and L3MBTL3, both of which comprise C-terminal SPM domains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both SCML2A and SCML2B recovered comparable amounts of USP7.
source: As a control, both SCML2A and SCML2B recovered comparable amounts of USP7, in good agreement with previous reports (Sowa et al., 2009) and as we also independently confirmed (Lecona et al. unpublished).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior work.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of BMI1 from the chromatin fraction of HeLa cells recovered preferentially the chromatin-associated and SPM-containing SCML2A isoform.
source: In keeping with these observations, immunoprecipitation (IP) of BMI1 from the chromatin fraction of HeLa cells recovered preferentially the chromatin-associated and SPM-containing SCML2A isoform (Figure 4B, compare top and bottom band in lane 4 vs lane 1 or lane 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Artificial tethering of both SCML2A and SCML2B to an integrated reporter resulted in a dose-dependent repression of transcription.
source: Consistent with the classification of SCML2 as a PcG (and therefore repressive) gene, artificial tethering of both SCML2A and SCML2B to an integrated reporter using the DNA-binding domain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Gal4p (Vaquero et al., 2004) resulted in a dose-dependent repression of transcription (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Only tethering of SCML2A but not SCML2B caused an increase in BMI1 recruitment to the UAS-containing reporter.
source: However, only tethering of SCML2A but not SCML2B caused an increase in BMI1 recruitment to the UAS-containing reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), confirming that the SPM domain is required for interacting with BMI1 and suggesting that SCML2A contributes to PRC1 targeting.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Recruitment of BMI1 was not necessary for SCML2-mediated repression in the tethering context.
source: On the other hand, recruitment of BMI1 was not necessary for SCML2-mediated repression in this context.
evidence: This is stated in the results and inferred from the observation that SCML2B represses transcription without recruiting BMI1.

claim: Both the MBT domains and the SPM domain contribute to the repressive activity of SCM in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this observation, both the MBT domains and the SPM domain contribute to the repressive activity of SCM in Drosophila (Roseman et al., 2001; Peterson et al., 2004; Grimm et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: More than 30% (781 out of 2479 total) of SCML2-enriched regions (ERs) were located in the vicinity (<10 kb) of the transcription start site (TSS) of protein-coding genes.
source: In these cells, more than 30% (781 out of 2479 total) of SCML2-enriched regions (ERs) were located in the vicinity (<10 kb) of the transcription start site (TSS) of protein-coding genes (Figure 4D), consistent with a role for SCML2 in gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SCML2 targets were significantly enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to transcriptional regulation, development, and differentiation.
source: SCML2 targets were significantly enriched for gene ontology (GO) terms related to transcriptional regulation, development, and differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1A), as observed for targets of the Polycomb repressive machinery in other systems (Schuettengruber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SCML2 and BMI1 co-occupied several promoters, including those of transcription factors RUNX1, IKZF2, and DMRT1.
source: SCML2 and BMI1 co-occupied several promoters, including those of transcription factors RUNX1, IKZF2, and DMRT1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1.
source: Overall, SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1 (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1B), almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119, hypergeometric distribution).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The overlap between SCML2 and BMI1 target genes was almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119).
source: Overall, SCML2 shared ∼46% of its target genes with BMI1 (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1B), almost four times more than expected by chance (p=2.5 × 10−119, hypergeometric distribution).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the statistical analysis of the overlap shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The overlap between SCML2 and BMI1 target genes became more pronounced as a function of decreasing p-values for the ERs.
source: This overlap became more pronounced as a function of decreasing p-values for the ERs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that many of the SCML2-only or BMI1-only sites were false positives due to noise in the ChIP-seq signal.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: SCML2ΔRBR was lost from several target genes.
source: Visual inspection of ChIP-seq profiles revealed that SCML2ΔRBR was lost from several target genes (Figure 5A), suggesting that the RBR, and presumably RNA–protein interactions might participate in the recruitment or stabilization of SCML2 on chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A smaller number of SCML2 ERs exhibited SCML2AΔRBR levels comparable to WT.
source: A smaller number of SCML2 ERs, including the ER near the RUNX1 TSS, exhibited SCML2AΔRBR levels comparable to WT (Figure 5A), consistent with the existence of RNA-independent pathways of SCML2A recruitment at some loci.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The N3–SCML2ΔRBR ChIP-seq signal was much weaker than WT when all significant ERs for SCML2 WT were combined in a single meta-ER plot.
source: Nonetheless, RBR-independent ERs constituted a small proportion of the total SCML2 binding profile, because the N3–SCML2ΔRBR ChIP-seq signal was much weaker than WT when all significant (p<10−5 according to MACS 1.4.0rc2) ERs for SCML2 WT were combined in a single meta-ER plot (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the meta-ER plot shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Partial replacement of endogenous SCML2 with SCML2AΔRBR resulted in a decreased, albeit not abolished, accumulation of BMI1 at several of the target sites.
source: Consistent with our observations that SCML2A colocalizes with BMI1 (Figure 4E,F) and can recruit it to chromatin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), partial replacement of endogenous SCML2 with SCML2AΔRBR resulted in a decreased, albeit not abolished, accumulation of BMI1 at several of the target sites (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: Out of 148 high-confidence ERs obtained from the triple intersection of SCML2, HA, and BMI1 ERs, a majority displayed losses in SCML2 binding in the absence of the RBR and many also had decreased BMI1 occupancy.
source: When inspected at the level of individual genomic regions, out of 148 high-confidence ERs obtained from the triple intersection of SCML2, HA, and BMI1 ERs, a majority displayed losses in SCML2 binding in the absence of the RBR and many also had decreased BMI1 occupancy (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity.
source: From this set of experiments, we conclude that SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity and that the presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: The presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
source: From this set of experiments, we conclude that SCML2 is recruited to a subset of target genes through a process that requires its RNA-binding activity and that the presence of mutant SCML2AΔRBR that is not chromatin-bound causes a partial release of BMI1 and, presumably, PRC1 from chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Only in the case of WT SCML2A, RNA could be detected in the co-IP.
source: To this end, we performed HA IPs in 293T-REx expressing N3-tagged SCML2A WT, ΔRBR, or the N3 tag alone. Although comparable amounts of WT and ΔRBR protein were recovered, only in the case of WT SCML2A, we could detect co-IP of RNA (Figure 6A,B), which we subjected to deep sequencing (RIP followed by sequencing, RIP-seq).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RIP data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Several specific interactions distinguished the set of RNAs recovered in RIPs for SCML2A WT from all other controls.
source: Although overall abundant lincRNAs were more likely to be detected by RIP-seq, several specific interactions distinguished the set of RNAs recovered in RIPs for SCML2A WT from all other controls (Figure 6C), demonstrating the specificity of RNA binding by SCML2 in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cell differentiation caused a measurable shift in the pool of lincRNAs associated with SCML2.
source: Indeed, cell differentiation caused a measurable shift in the pool of lincRNAs associated with SCML2 (Figure 6D), suggesting that in addition to intrinsic binding preferences, cellular context may also determine which RNAs bind to SCML2 and, in turn, how its function and distribution on chromatin is affected by these interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Several unannotated ncRNAs were enriched in SCML2 RIPs compared to input RNA and were transcribed near SCML2 ERs.
source: We also found several examples of unannotated ncRNAs that were enriched in SCML2 RIPs compared to input RNA and were transcribed near SCML2 ERs (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E), which is consistent with the notion that some ncRNAs interacting with SCML2 might act in cis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo.
source: Thus, SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo. These interactions are specific and they are also dynamic, likely reflecting the need to adjust SCML2 localization or regulation as the cells transition from one transcriptional and/or epigenetic state to another.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the RIP-seq experiments.

claim: SCML2-RNA interactions are specific and dynamic.
source: Thus, SCML2 associates with annotated and unannotated lncRNAs via the RBR in vivo. These interactions are specific and they are also dynamic, likely reflecting the need to adjust SCML2 localization or regulation as the cells transition from one transcriptional and/or epigenetic state to another.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the RIP-seq experiments.

claim: A total of 530 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified after SCML2 knockdown using a cutoff of p<0.2.
source: We generated genome-wide expression profiles by RNA-seq in two biological replicates and combined all data sets to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Using a loose cutoff of p<0.2, we identified a total of 530 DEGs of which a significant fraction overlapped (p=1.4 × 10−4, hypergeometric distribution) with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A significant fraction of DEGs after SCML2 knockdown overlapped with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (p=1.4 × 10−4).
source: We generated genome-wide expression profiles by RNA-seq in two biological replicates and combined all data sets to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Using a loose cutoff of p<0.2, we identified a total of 530 DEGs of which a significant fraction overlapped (p=1.4 × 10−4, hypergeometric distribution) with the set of genes associated with an SCML2 ER (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A majority (341) of DEGs after SCML2 knockdown were upregulated.
source: In keeping with the postulated repressive function of SCML2, a majority (341) of these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1C) and this subset accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Upregulated genes after SCML2 knockdown accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin.
source: In keeping with the postulated repressive function of SCML2, a majority (341) of these genes were upregulated (Supplementary file 1C) and this subset accounted for ∼86% of the DEGs associated with SCML2 occupancy on chromatin (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The levels of BMI1 on chromatin were unaffected after SCML2 knockdown, even at sites that lost SCML2 occupancy.
source: Given that SCML2A can recruit BMI1, and therefore PRC1, to an artificial reporter and that PRC1 is generally thought as the effector of Polycomb-mediated repression (Simon and Kingston, 2009), we hypothesized that the changes in transcriptional activity observed above might be secondary to a loss of BMI1 from SCML2-bound genes. Unexpectedly, this was not the case. In fact, the levels of BMI1 on chromatin were unaffected even when we analyzed only the 520 sites that lost SCML2 occupancy after SCML2 knockdown (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: In the absence of SCML2, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
source: Together with the observation that SCML2B retains the ability to repress a reporter independent of BMI1 recruitment (Figure 4C), these findings reinforce the notion that SCML2 represses transcription by itself, and that, in its absence, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: SCML2 represses transcription by itself.
source: Together with the observation that SCML2B retains the ability to repress a reporter independent of BMI1 recruitment (Figure 4C), these findings reinforce the notion that SCML2 represses transcription by itself, and that, in its absence, PRC1 alone is not sufficient to maintain repression at all target genes.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding.
source: Here, we have unveiled two mechanisms by which SCML2A contributes to PRC1 function: (1) SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding, as evidenced by loss of BMI1 upon overexpression of SCML2AΔRBR, recruitment of BMI1 by SCML2A at artificial tethering sites, and the weak association of SCML2B to chromatin; and (2) SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
source: Here, we have unveiled two mechanisms by which SCML2A contributes to PRC1 function: (1) SCML2 and PRC1 cooperate in chromatin binding, as evidenced by loss of BMI1 upon overexpression of SCML2AΔRBR, recruitment of BMI1 by SCML2A at artificial tethering sites, and the weak association of SCML2B to chromatin; and (2) SCML2 enforces repression at some target sites independent of the presence of PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: RNA binding plays a role in SCML2 function, as it is required for its localization to chromatin.
source: In addition, our results show that RNA binding also plays a role in SCML2 function, as it is required for its localization to chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The interaction of SCM and PRC1 in Drosophila relies on the C-terminal SPM domain.
source: In Drosophila, the interaction of SCM and PRC1 relies on the C-terminal SPM domain (Peterson et al., 2004) and our results show that a similar mechanism is conserved in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A similar mechanism of SCM-PRC1 interaction via the SPM domain is conserved in humans.
source: In Drosophila, the interaction of SCM and PRC1 relies on the C-terminal SPM domain (Peterson et al., 2004) and our results show that a similar mechanism is conserved in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: SCML2 is part of PRC1.2, which does not contain BMI1.
source: The former might reflect the complexity of PRC1 subtypes in mammals and the fact that SCML2 is also part of PRC1.2, which does not contain BMI1 (Gao et al., 2012); the latter is likely due to the higher sensitivity of the BMI1 antibody, although we cannot exclude that some BMI1 target sites are devoid of SCML2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SCML2 might directly enforce gene repression via the MBT domain, which binds to methylated histone tails.
source: This PRC1-independent silencing may be mediated by the MBT domain, which binds to methylated histone tails (Grimm et al., 2007; Santiveri et al., 2008) and, in the case of L3MBTL1, represses transcription via chromatin compaction (Trojer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on prior work on MBT domains.

claim: The MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression.
source: In fact, the MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression (Grimm et al., 2007), and our results show that the MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2.
source: In fact, the MBT domain of SCM in Drosophila is important for repression (Grimm et al., 2007), and our results show that the MBT domain contributes to the chromatin localization of SCML2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the salt fractionation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro.
source: Despite the fact that the 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro (Figures 1 and 2), prediction algorithms failed to detect known protein folds or the propensity to form secondary structures in this region, suggesting that, in isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the in vitro binding data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
source: Despite the fact that the 74-residue fragment containing the RBR is both necessary and sufficient for RNA binding in vitro (Figures 1 and 2), prediction algorithms failed to detect known protein folds or the propensity to form secondary structures in this region, suggesting that, in isolation, the RBR remains unstructured.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the failure of prediction algorithms to detect structure.

claim: Induced fit is a common feature of RNA–protein interactions.
source: This is not entirely unexpected, considering that induced fit is a common feature of RNA–protein interactions (Williamson, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The fragile X syndrome protein FMR1/FMRP contains an arginine-rich stretch that is disordered in solution but becomes ordered in presence of an RNA ligand.
source: For example, the fragile X syndrome protein FMR1/FMRP contains an arginine-rich stretch that is disordered in solution but becomes ordered in presence of an RNA ligand (Phan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1.
source: Although the RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1, its disruption resulted not only in a delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin (Figure 3), but also in decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A).

claim: Disruption of the RBR resulted in delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin and decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes.
source: Although the RBR was dispensable for the interaction with PRC1, its disruption resulted not only in a delocalization of SCML2A from chromatin (Figure 3), but also in decreased PRC1 occupancy at several target genes (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the fractionation and ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Nucleoplasmic SCML2ΔRBR might function in a dominant negative fashion, titrating PRC1 away from chromatin.
source: This observation is intriguing in view of the fact that short-term SCML2 knockdown did not affect BMI1 localization, and suggests that nucleoplasmic SCML2ΔRBR, being still capable of interacting with BMI1 through the SPM domain, might function in a dominant negative fashion, titrating PRC1 away from chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the observation that SCML2ΔRBR interacts with BMI1 but is not chromatin-bound.

claim: SCML2–RNA interactions appeared to be specific in vivo.
source: Despite promiscuous RNA binding in vitro, SCML2–RNA interactions appeared to be specific in vivo, as demonstrated by the following observations: (1) the profile of lincRNAs enriched in the SCML2A WT RIP-seq was unique and distinct from input and control samples (Figure 6C); (2) the lincRNAs associated with SCML2 changed upon cellular differentiation (Figure 6D); and (3) several divergently transcribed ncRNAs were enriched in SCML2 RIPs although the coding mRNAs originating from the same locus were not (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the RIP-seq data shown in Figures 6C-E.

claim: Physical proximity on chromatin alone was not the main determinant of SCML2–RNA interactions.
source: The latter also demonstrates that physical proximity on chromatin alone was not the main determinant of SCML2–RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the observation that divergent ncRNAs but not nearby mRNAs are enriched in SCML2 RIPs.

claim: The RBR is likely required to mediate the interactions with RNAs in vivo.
source: Furthermore, the RBR is likely required to mediate the interactions with these RNAs, given that immunoprecipitation of the ΔRBR mutant recovered less RNA than the WT (Figure 6B) and that the few detected ΔRBR-associated RNAs were undistinguishable from those obtained in empty tag-expressing cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the RIP data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The RBR of SCML2A contributes to its recruitment either by interacting with trans-acting RNAs transcribed from distant intergenic loci, or by recognizing cis-acting ncRNAs.
source: We propose that the RBR of SCML2A contributes to its recruitment either by interacting with trans-acting RNAs transcribed from distant intergenic loci, or by recognizing cis-acting ncRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed model based on the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS have a demonstrated role in gene regulation.
source: The latter may include divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS, some of which have a demonstrated role in gene regulation (Faghihi and Wahlestedt, 2009; Modarresi et al., 2012), or promoter-associated ncRNAs that originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand (Kapranov et al., 2007), similar to the ncRNAs reported to bind PRC2 via SUZ12 (Kanhere et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Promoter-associated ncRNAs originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand.
source: The latter may include divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS, some of which have a demonstrated role in gene regulation (Faghihi and Wahlestedt, 2009; Modarresi et al., 2012), or promoter-associated ncRNAs that originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand (Kapranov et al., 2007), similar to the ncRNAs reported to bind PRC2 via SUZ12 (Kanhere et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ncRNAs have been reported to bind PRC2 via SUZ12.
source: The latter may include divergent and overlapping antisense ncRNAs that originate downstream of the TSS, some of which have a demonstrated role in gene regulation (Faghihi and Wahlestedt, 2009; Modarresi et al., 2012), or promoter-associated ncRNAs that originate near the TSS of coding genes and are transcribed from the same strand (Kapranov et al., 2007), similar to the ncRNAs reported to bind PRC2 via SUZ12 (Kanhere et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A significant spatial association between the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq signals at the genome-wide level could not be detected.
source: We note that despite the examples shown (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E) and several others, we could not detect a significant spatial association between the RIP-seq and ChIP-seq signals at the genome-wide level (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on unpublished data.

claim: Only a subset of the SCML2-associated ncRNAs act in cis.
source: This might be due to the fact that only a subset of the SCML2-associated ncRNAs act in cis or to the intrinsically noisy nature of the RIP-seq signal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation to explain the lack of genome-wide spatial association between RIP-seq and ChIP-seq signals.

claim: SCML2A is retained at target genes through the interaction with PRC1.
source: We propose that SCML2A is then retained at target genes through the interaction with PRC1 and that, in turn, SCML2A contributes to stabilizing PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: SCML2A contributes to stabilizing PRC1.
source: We propose that SCML2A is then retained at target genes through the interaction with PRC1 and that, in turn, SCML2A contributes to stabilizing PRC1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed model based on the findings.
